notes.meaning: Ezekiel receives a new message from God. In this chapter the prophet sets aside his usual picture-language and speaks very plainly. The subject matters for both people's comfort and God's honor: how God judges each person.

The people in exile had a popular saying. The sour grapes stand for the parents' sins, and the children's sore teeth stand for the suffering that followed. They meant, "We are being punished for what our ancestors did, not for anything we did." God had warned that he would punish a nation's sins over generations, but the people twisted that into a complaint that God was unfair to them.

God makes a solemn promise by his own life. The saying will be silenced. God will make it plain to everyone that the people are suffering for their own sins, so they can no longer blame their fathers. Keil adds that God's later mercy and forgiveness will also convince them that his judgments were fair.

Every person belongs to God, parent and child alike. Calvin says this shows God's fatherly love for the people he made, not only his right to rule them. So God will not punish one person for another's sin. The person who sins is the one who dies. Here "death" means being cut off from God's favor, the full punishment the law warned of.

God now gives a series of examples, starting with a good man. Doing "what is just and right" means being honest and fair with others. It also means standing up for people who are being wronged. The list that follows names the common sins of that time, which a godly man would stay away from.

"Eating at the mountain" means joining feasts held at hilltop shrines where sacrifices were made to idols. The good man does not even look to idols for help, including the idols that were popular among God's own people. He also stays sexually pure. He does not commit adultery, and he keeps the law about not sleeping with his wife during her period (Leviticus 18:19).

He does not bully anyone. When a poor man leaves something with him as a pledge for a loan, such as his coat or the tools he works with, he gives it back as the law required. He does not rob. He also does good: he feeds the hungry and clothes the poor. Calling it "his" bread reminds us that what we own is meant to be shared with people in need.

The word for usury literally means "biting." It means charging interest that eats away at a poor neighbor. The point is not to profit from someone else's hard times. The good man holds back from easy but crooked gain. When he settles disputes, he judges fairly and is not swayed by favoritism or fear.

Above all, he walks in God's ways and keeps God's laws faithfully and sincerely. God declares that such a man is righteous and "will surely live." Commentators take this to mean blessing in this life and, even more, life with God forever. Calvin and Matthew Henry add that no one keeps the law perfectly. Where we fall short, forgiveness comes through Christ.

Now suppose the good man has a violent son who does everything his father refused to do. It happens that godly parents have wicked children, even after good teaching and many prayers. Goodness does not run in the blood. Having a godly father makes the son's sin worse, not better.

The son crushes the poor, robs, worships idols and lends at cruel interest. Will his father's goodness save him? No. "His blood will be on his own head" means the blame for his ruin is his alone. A son suffers for his father's sins only if he copies them and does not repent.

Next, the wicked son has a son of his own. This boy looks hard at his father's sins and chooses not to copy them. The Hebrew repeats the word for "see," showing how carefully he must look. Children are often blind to their parents' faults. Bible examples include good King Hezekiah, son of wicked Ahaz, and Josiah, son of Amon.

His life matches the good man described earlier, almost word for word. He turns from his father's sins and follows his grandfather's good example instead. He avoids idols, adultery and robbery. He also feeds the hungry and clothes the naked.

"Withholds his hand from the poor" means he refuses to take advantage of the weak, even when he could easily get away with it. Matthew Henry pictures him easing the burdens his father had put on others. God's verdict is clear: he will not die for his father's sin. He will surely live.

The cruel father, though, will die for his own sin. He robbed his own people and did no good with the power he had. His wickedness may have cost his son money or standing in the world. But it cannot harm the son's standing with God.

God answers a question the people might raise: "Why shouldn't the son share his father's guilt?" Keil suggests they were leaning on the law's warning about the sins of the fathers. God's answer is simple. The son did what was right, so he will live. Matthew Henry adds that a curse on a family can be broken by turning to God.

God sums up the rule: each person answers for his own sin, as the law already taught (Deuteronomy 24:16). This does not clash with God "visiting the sins of the fathers on the children." That warning is about children who hate God and walk in their parents' sins. Each person reaps what his own life has sown, whether blessing or punishment.

differ.view: All people share in Adam's sin and are born with a sinful nature that is enough, on its own, to condemn them. Still, no one is condemned as an innocent, because each person carries that guilt himself. Ezekiel is speaking here of adults.
Everyone is born with a fallen nature, but no one is condemned for that alone. Only those who refuse God's grace and go on in sin are lost.

notes.meaning: Even a wicked man can change course. If he turns from all his sins and begins obeying God, he will live. Real repentance (turning away from sin) is wholehearted. It turns from every sin, not just some, and turns toward obeying God. God holds out this hope because despair only makes people harder.

None of his past sins will be brought up against him. They are fully forgiven and remembered no more. He lives "in" the good he now does, not "because of" it, as if it paid for his sins. His new life is the fruit of faith and a gift of God's grace.
God opens his heart. He does not enjoy seeing the wicked die. What he wants is for them to turn and live. He is far more ready to forgive than to punish.

differ.view: Here God speaks of his open call to all to repent, not of his hidden plan of choosing whom he will save. Both are true, even though we cannot fully see how they fit together.
Since God takes no pleasure in a sinner's death, he cannot have decided to leave anyone in sin and then condemn them for what they could not avoid.

notes.meaning: Now comes the warning. If a righteous man turns away and lives like the wicked, his past good deeds will not save him. He will die in his sin. A good start is not enough; we must keep going to the end.

differ.view: The verse describes someone who only looked righteous to others. Those truly born again by God's Spirit will never fully fall away, so the warning keeps believers watchful.
The verse speaks of real righteousness. A truly holy person can turn away so completely that he is finally lost.

notes.meaning: The people complain, "God's way is not fair." The Hebrew pictures something not properly weighed on a scale. God turns the charge around: it is their ways that are out of balance. They lived in sin yet expected to be treated as righteous. In every dispute with God, he is right and we are wrong.
God repeats the warning to drive it home. The person who leaves righteousness for sin dies because of his own sin. God is simply judging him by what he has done.

God repeats the good news too. The wicked person who turns from his sin and does right saves his life. Turning begins when he "considers" his ways, like coming to his senses and seeing where his path leads. Then he turns from all his sins. He is welcomed back into God's favor.
Even after all this, the people still call God unfair. God answers again: the unfairness is in their ways, not his. People object to God's justice because they do not want to see it.

God will judge each person by his own life. So he calls them to repent, which means to turn their hearts back to him and leave their sins behind. The Hebrew plays on the word "turn": "turn and return." Calvin says this means an inner change of heart first, then a changed life. Otherwise their sin will become a trap that brings them down.

God calls them to throw away their sins and get a new heart and a new spirit. No one can create these by his own power; God gives them, as he promised (Ezekiel 11:19). But people can and should come to God to receive them. Matthew Henry quotes Augustine: God commands us to do what we can and to pray for what we cannot. Then God pleads, "Why should you die?"

differ.view: The command shows people their duty, not their ability. A new heart is wholly God's work, and the command drives people to seek his Spirit.
God gives a new heart to all who earnestly call on him for it. It is by grace alone, yet God speaks as if they make it, because they come to receive it. Wesley puts it as "Let me do it in you."

notes.meaning: The chapter ends with God's heart laid bare. He takes no pleasure in anyone's death. Keil notes that people living in sin are already lying in death and can only find life by turning to God. So God's last word is an invitation: turn and live!
